newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Reform row deepens in Bulgaria ruling party.
newsitem.headline: Reform row deepens in Bulgaria ruling party.

text.p: Reformists in Bulgaria's ruling party, reeling from a presidential election defeat, on Wednesday urged the government to reshuffle its ranks and commit itself clearly to IMF reforms to ward off economic collapse.

A visiting International Monetary Fund (IMF) mission discussed pegging the collapsing lev to the dollar or the mark through a currency board to help the authorities win back control of the economy and restore confidence.
But an IMF statement sounded a warning that the measure would succeed "only if it is supported by a sufficiently austere budget and broad social and political consensus".

The ruling Bulgarian Socialist Party was stunned by the decisive victory in Sunday's run-off for the presidency of opposition candidate Petar Stoyanov. He won almost 60 percent of votes against the 40 percent polled by Socialist Culture Minister Ivan Marazov.
On Tuesday, the party daily Douma published a letter signed by 19 senior Socialists, including party vice-chairman Yanaki Stoilov, calling for a new cabinet and extensive policy reform.
Stoilov told Reuters on Wednesday that the party leadership would meet on Monday to discuss what needed to be done.
"It is clear that structural reform in Bulgaria has no alternative but we think there are different ways, I should say better ways, for implementing it," he said.

Asked whether cabinet changes should include replacing the prime minister and party chairman Zhan Videnov, he said: "All questions are absolutely open and subject to discussion, they can be discussed without any limits in the coming plenum."
Reformist foreign minister Georgi Pirinski did not sign the letter but told Douma ideological considerations had hindered the government's ability to carry out IMF-prescribed reforms.
"And now we are reaping the fruits of this. We are on the verge of a collapse of the financial system with all its attendant crisis consequences," Pirinski said.
The Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) is made up mainly of ex-communists, who renamed their party after former leader Todor Zhivkov was toppled in 1989 and remain closer to Moscow than to Brussels.
The Socialists' veteran former chairman Alexander Lilov said swift action was needed to form a cabinet able to steer the country through the hardships of the coming winter.
"I believe and I insist that a new government of the democratic left should be formed before the winter. This is precisely the reason for our proposal," Lilov told reporters on Wednesday.

The lev has collapsed from 70 to the dollar at the start of the year to 249 on Wednesday. Annual inflation is forecast at 240 percent and many Bulgarians say they are having to choose between heating their homes and putting food on the table.
The IMF mission is discussing terms for release of a $115 million credit vital to avert default on Bulgaria's $10 billion foreign debt.

The funds have twice been delayed because of the government's failure to meet reform targets which include curbing inflation, stabilising the exchange rate, speeding up privatisation and closing loss-making enterprises.
